```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(car)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
pm <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1zf1xk-7pOoSnEwGvGsNVa6XejFoPFzdJ", quiet = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"))
summer_temp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1byhsYTBnqegfPGsZWtAHH4pZgGbSTr_s", quiet = TRUE)
mobility <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1YbCNVR5K8jDF5HOKHcoJ25gz7VkRvDHa", quiet = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"))
acs <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ffMbuX4ZQ8vuZK9uwFOBe61bEbKfKg1j", quiet = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"),
         low_inc = ifelse(low_inc == 1, "low income", "not low income"),
         high_commute = ifelse(high_commute == 1, "high commute", "low commute"))

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pm_key <- t.test(meanpm_2016_2020 ~ rural, data = pm, var.equal = TRUE)
temp_key <- t.test(summer_temp$av_summer_2010_2020, summer_temp$av_summer_2000_2010, paired = TRUE)
```

This tutorial runs over two class days. Day 1 covers t-tests and Day 2 covers the chi-square test. Each day has its own walkthrough, partner practice and index card.

## Day 1 Walkthrough: T-Tests {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in the Day 1 partner practice.

### Step 1: Load the Data

::: {.why}
`pm` has the mean daily PM2.5 (µg/m³) from 2016 to 2020 for `r fmt(nrow(pm), 0)` North Carolina census tracts, from the [CDC Environmental Public Health Tracking Network](https://ephtracking.cdc.gov/), with a rural or non-rural label. `summer_temp` has the average summer temperature (°F) at `r nrow(summer_temp)` locations for 2000 to 2010 and for 2010 to 2020, from [TerraClimate](https://www.climatologylab.org/terraclimate.html). We treat both as natural samples.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(car)

#census tract PM2.5, 2016-2020
pm <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1zf1xk-7pOoSnEwGvGsNVa6XejFoPFzdJ") |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"))

#summer temperature at 480 locations
summer_temp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1byhsYTBnqegfPGsZWtAHH4pZgGbSTr_s")
```

### Step 2: Check the Assumptions

::: {.why}
A t-test needs a continuous variable, independent observations and a roughly normal sampling distribution of the mean. Spatial data are rarely independent, so keep that limit in mind. With `r fmt(nrow(pm), 0)` tracts, the Central Limit Theorem covers the normality assumption even though the histogram is skewed.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of mean PM2.5 for North Carolina census tracts. Values run from about 5 to 9 micrograms per cubic meter and are skewed left, with most tracts between 7 and 9."}
ggplot(pm, aes(x = meanpm_2016_2020)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Mean PM2.5, 2016-2020 (µg/m³)", y = "Number of tracts")
```

### Step 3: One-Sample T-Test

::: {.why}
A one-sample t-test compares a mean with a fixed value. The EPA's annual PM2.5 standard is 9.0 µg/m³. H0: the mean tract PM2.5 is 9.0. H1: it is less than 9.0.
:::

```{r}
t.test(pm$meanpm_2016_2020, mu = 9.0, alternative = "less")
```

### Step 4: Two-Sample T-Test and Effect Size

::: {.why}
A two-sample t-test compares the means of two groups. Check equal variance first with Levene's test. If its p-value is below 0.05, add `var.equal = FALSE` (Welch's test). H0: rural and non-rural tracts have the same mean PM2.5.
:::

```{r}
leveneTest(meanpm_2016_2020 ~ rural, data = pm)

pm_test <- t.test(meanpm_2016_2020 ~ rural, data = pm, var.equal = TRUE)
pm_test

#effect size: the difference between the two group means, in µg/m³
pm_test$estimate
diff(pm_test$estimate)
```

The p-value says a difference this large would be very unlikely if H0 were true. The effect size says how big the difference is: rural tracts average `r fmt(abs(diff(pm_key$estimate)))` µg/m³ less PM2.5 than non-rural tracts (`r fmt(pm_key$estimate[2])` vs. `r fmt(pm_key$estimate[1])`).

### Step 5: Paired T-Test

::: {.why}
A paired t-test is for two measurements of the same places. It tests whether the mean of the differences is 0. H0: the mean change in summer temperature from 2000-2010 to 2010-2020 is 0.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of the change in average summer temperature at 480 North Carolina locations from 2000-2010 to 2010-2020. Every change is positive, from about 0.75 to 1.4 degrees F, with most between 1.0 and 1.35."}
summer_temp <- summer_temp |> mutate(diff = av_summer_2010_2020 - av_summer_2000_2010)

ggplot(summer_temp, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Change in summer temperature (°F)", y = "Number of locations")

#the estimate in the output is the effect size: the mean change in °F
t.test(summer_temp$av_summer_2010_2020, summer_temp$av_summer_2000_2010, paired = TRUE)
```

## Day 1 Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners use workplace mobility for North Carolina's 100 counties in 2020, from the [Google COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports](https://www.google.com/covid19/mobility/). `workplace_change` is the percent change in visits to workplaces from March to May 2020, compared with before the pandemic, and `workplace_change_may_dec` is the same for May to December 2020. Negative numbers mean fewer visits. Partner A compares rural and non-rural counties, and Partner B compares the two time periods. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#county mobility, 2020 (both partners)
mobility <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1YbCNVR5K8jDF5HOKHcoJ25gz7VkRvDHa") |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"))
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Rural vs. Non-Rural

1. Write H0 and H1 for comparing `workplace_change` in rural and non-rural counties.
2. Plot a histogram of `workplace_change`. *(Step 2)*
3. Run Levene's test, then the two-sample t-test. *(Step 4)*
4. Pull out the two group means and the difference between them. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your hypotheses, p-value, group means and effect size to Day 1 Together.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: March to May vs. May to December

1. Write H0 and H1 for comparing `workplace_change_may_dec` with `workplace_change` in the same counties.
2. Make a column of the differences and plot its histogram. *(Step 5)*
3. Run the paired t-test. *(Step 5)*
4. Pull out the mean difference. *(Step 5)*

When you finish, bring your hypotheses, p-value and effect size to Day 1 Together.
:::
::::

## Day 1 Together {#together}

1. Fill in the table.
2. Which result is larger in real terms, the gap between rural and non-rural counties or the change over time?
3. Counties next to each other tend to have similar mobility. Which assumption does that break?

| Test | H0 | p-value | Effect size (percentage points) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rural vs. non-rural (Partner A) | | | |
| March-May vs. May-December (Partner B) | | | |

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, copy the table, and add two or three sentences describing each result in plain language, with its effect size, for example "rural counties dropped ___ points less than non-rural counties."
:::

## Day 2 Walkthrough: Chi-Square Test {#walkthrough-2}

### Step 1: Load the Data

::: {.why}
`acs` has three yes-or-no labels for `r fmt(nrow(acs), 0)` North Carolina census tracts from the [American Community Survey](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs.html): rural or not (`rural`), low income or not (`low_inc`), and long average commutes or not (`high_commute`). The chi-square test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

#census tracts with three categorical labels
acs <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ffMbuX4ZQ8vuZK9uwFOBe61bEbKfKg1j") |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"),
         low_inc = ifelse(low_inc == 1, "low income", "not low income"),
         high_commute = ifelse(high_commute == 1, "high commute", "low commute"))
```

### Step 2: Contingency Table and Row Percentages

::: {.why}
H0: rural status and low-income status are independent. The row percentages show the effect size: how much more common low-income tracts are in one group than in the other.
:::

```{r}
inc_table <- table(acs$rural, acs$low_inc)
inc_table

#share of each row in each column
prop.table(inc_table, margin = 1)
```

### Step 3: Run the Test

```{r}
inc_test <- chisq.test(inc_table)
inc_test
```

### Step 4: Check the Expected Counts

::: {.why}
The chi-square test needs an expected count of at least 5 in every cell. The expected counts are what the table would look like if the two variables were unrelated.
:::

```{r}
inc_test$expected
```

`r fmt(100 * prop.table(table(acs$rural, acs$low_inc), 1)["rural", "low income"], 1)`% of rural tracts are low income, compared with `r fmt(100 * prop.table(table(acs$rural, acs$low_inc), 1)["non-rural", "low income"], 1)`% of non-rural tracts, and the p-value is far below 0.05, so we reject H0.

## Day 2 Partner Practice {#partner-practice-2}

Both partners use the same `acs` tracts. Partner A tests whether rural status and commute are related, and Partner B tests whether income and commute are related. Each task tells you in parentheses which Day 2 step to reuse.

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Rural and Commute

1. Write H0 and H1 for `rural` and `high_commute`.
2. Make the contingency table and the row percentages. *(Step 2)*
3. Run the chi-square test. *(Step 3)*
4. Check the expected counts. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your table, the percentage of each group with a high commute, X-squared and the p-value to Day 2 Together.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Income and Commute

1. Write H0 and H1 for `low_inc` and `high_commute`.
2. Make the contingency table and the row percentages. *(Step 2)*
3. Run the chi-square test. *(Step 3)*
4. Check the expected counts. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your table, the percentage of each group with a high commute, X-squared and the p-value to Day 2 Together.
:::
::::

2. One of you should reject H0 and one should not. Use your row percentages to explain why.
3. A statistically significant result can still be a small difference. How big is the difference in Partner B's percentages?

| Variables | % high commute in each group | X-squared | p-value | Reject H0? |

| Rural and commute (Partner A) | | | | |
| Income and commute (Partner B) | | | | |

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
a_test <- t.test(workplace_change ~ rural, data = mobility, var.equal = TRUE)
a_lev <- leveneTest(workplace_change ~ rural, data = mobility)
b_test <- t.test(mobility$workplace_change_may_dec, mobility$workplace_change, paired = TRUE)
pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p, 3))
tab_a <- table(acs$rural, acs$high_commute); pa <- prop.table(tab_a, 1); ca <- chisq.test(tab_a)
tab_b <- table(acs$low_inc, acs$high_commute); pb <- prop.table(tab_b, 1); cb <- chisq.test(tab_b)
```

### Day 1

Partner A. H0: rural and non-rural counties have the same mean `workplace_change`. Levene's p-value is `r fmt(a_lev[1, "Pr(>F)"], 2)`, so equal variance is fine. The t-test p-value is `r pv(a_test$p.value)`. Non-rural counties averaged `r fmt(a_test$estimate[1], 1)`% and rural counties `r fmt(a_test$estimate[2], 1)`%, so non-rural counties cut workplace visits by `r fmt(abs(diff(a_test$estimate)), 1)` percentage points more.

Partner B. H0: the mean difference between the two periods is 0. The paired t-test p-value is `r pv(b_test$p.value)`. The mean difference is `r fmt(b_test$estimate, 1)` percentage points: from May to December, workplace visits were about `r fmt(b_test$estimate, 1)` points closer to normal than in March to May.

Both results are significant and of similar size, about 8 to 9 percentage points. Counties are not independent of their neighbors, so the independence assumption is broken and the p-values are likely too small.

### Day 2

| Variables | % high commute in each group | X-squared | p-value | Reject H0? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rural and commute | rural `r fmt(100 * pa["rural", "high commute"], 1)`%, non-rural `r fmt(100 * pa["non-rural", "high commute"], 1)`% | `r fmt(ca$statistic)` | `r pv(ca$p.value)` | No |
| Income and commute | low income `r fmt(100 * pb["low income", "high commute"], 1)`%, not low income `r fmt(100 * pb["not low income", "high commute"], 1)`% | `r fmt(cb$statistic)` | `r pv(cb$p.value)` | Yes |

Every expected count is well above 5. Rural and non-rural tracts have almost the same share of high-commute tracts, so Partner A fails to reject H0: these data show no relationship between rural status and commute. Low-income tracts are less likely to have high commutes, a difference of about `r round(100 * abs(pb["low income", "high commute"] - pb["not low income", "high commute"]))` percentage points. That is significant with this many tracts, but it is a modest difference.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mobility <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1YbCNVR5K8jDF5HOKHcoJ25gz7VkRvDHa") |>
  mutate(rural = ifelse(rural == 1, "rural", "non-rural"))

#### Day 1, Partner A: rural vs. non-rural ####
ggplot(mobility, aes(x = workplace_change)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Change in workplace visits, March-May 2020 (%)", y = "Number of counties")

leveneTest(workplace_change ~ rural, data = mobility)
a_test <- t.test(workplace_change ~ rural, data = mobility, var.equal = TRUE)
a_test
a_test$estimate
diff(a_test$estimate)

#### Day 1, Partner B: March-May vs. May-December ####
mobility <- mobility |> mutate(diff = workplace_change_may_dec - workplace_change)

ggplot(mobility, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "May-December minus March-May (percentage points)", y = "Number of counties")

t.test(mobility$workplace_change_may_dec, mobility$workplace_change, paired = TRUE)

#### Day 2, Partner A: rural and commute ####
tab_a <- table(acs$rural, acs$high_commute)
tab_a
prop.table(tab_a, margin = 1)
test_a <- chisq.test(tab_a)
test_a
test_a$expected

#### Day 2, Partner B: income and commute ####
tab_b <- table(acs$low_inc, acs$high_commute)
tab_b
prop.table(tab_b, margin = 1)
test_b <- chisq.test(tab_b)
test_b
test_b$expected
```
